newsitem.title: PERU: In Peru, guerrillas have long been deadly menace.
newsitem.headline: In Peru, guerrillas have long been deadly menace.

text.p: Plagued by a tragic history of violence and poverty, Peru has been bloodied for most of its recent history by guerrilla movements that autocratic President Alberto Fujimori thought he had all but wiped out.

The seizure of hundreds of hostages by guerrillas in the Japanese ambassador's residence on Tuesday night was the latest terror-driven twist in a tumultuous history that has made Peruvian rebels among the most feared in the world.

Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, risked a firestorm of international condemnation in April 1992 when he shut Congress, fired nearly half the Supreme Court and seized near-dictatorial powers to crush the rebels and push through radical reforms.

But he correctly gauged the mood of Peruvians, fed up with corrupt old-style politics and sickened with fear of the rural killings and urban bombings that had plagued Latin America's fourth biggest country during the guerrilla heyday of the late 1980s and early 1990s.

His crackdown almost immediately paid off. Two months after his "self-coup," Fujimori's police captured Victor Polay, leader of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA). That drove the Cuban-inspired movement mostly underground until the Japanese embassy storming.

Fujimori's maverick style scored another big success with the September 1992 arrest of Abimael Guzman, the revolutionary guru who headed the Maoist Shining Path rebels, a far more prominent and blood-thirsty group.

The arrests, and claims the two movements virtually collapsed in their aftermath, briefly sent Fujimori's popularity soaring and brought a flood of foreign investment into Peru. However, recent months have brought renewed rebel attacks, economic problems and doubts over Fujimori's claims to have slain the rebel threat.

The former agricultural engineer and university professor came from nowhere to win the presidency in 1990 and was swept back to power in April 1995. But some of his popularity has ebbed amid criticism of authoritarianism, the failure to strengthen Congress and the judiciary to balance his powers and stubbornly high levels of poverty and unemployment.

Although Peru has enjoyed some of the fastest growth rates in the world under Fujimori's tenure, more than four-fifths of the workforce remains jobless or under-employed and the economy has faltered badly over the past year.

Scarred by hyperinflation in the 1980s when its failure to repay debts made it a pariah of the international financial community, it remains one of Latin America's poorest nations. GDP per head is just $950 -- about a third of the level in wealthier Latin nations such as Brazil, Venezuela and Chile.
The mostly Indian population still speaks the ancestral Inca tongue Quechua and only one in 32 people has a telephone.

Rebels have managed to recruit in the dismal shantytowns surrounding the capital Lima as well as in the mountainous rural regions on the flanks of the Andes, where peasants, mostly of Indian stock, live in dire conditions.

Founded in 1984, the MRTA operates mainly in the Upper Huallaga Valley in eastern Peru, an area infested with drug traffickers. There it has clashed repeatedly with the rival Shining Path rebels over taxes from cocaine smugglers.
The MRTA is named after 18th century Indian rebel, Tupac Amaru, who led an uprising against Spanish conquerors in 1782.
